title: Residual Features and Unified Prediction Network for Single Stage Detection

problem.summary: In SSD-style single-stage detectors the shallow lower-layer feature maps that must detect small objects lack representation power, and they are structurally forced to carry low-level information forward while also producing high-level predictions; backbone gradients are deformed by direct training pressure, per-layer heads cannot share cross-scale context (Box-in-Box), and existing FPN/ResNet fixes cost the speed that defines one-stage detection.
statements: Lower-layer feature maps close to the input are too shallow to represent small objects for prediction.
Feature maps face a structural contradiction: delivering low-level information to the next layer while containing high-level abstraction for prediction.
Training the prediction heads directly on backbone feature maps causes unnecessary gradient deformations and learning instability.
Separate per-layer prediction modules cannot reflect contextual information from different scales, producing the Box-in-Box problem of redundant overlapping boxes.
Prior context-injection fixes (DSSD, FPN) increase computational complexity and reduce detection speed.

evidence.quote: However, the feature maps in the lower layers close to the input which are responsible for detecting small objects in a single stage detector have a problem of insufficient representation power because they are too shallow.
There is also a structural contradiction that the feature maps have to deliver low-level information to next layers as well as contain high-level abstraction for prediction.

SSD has the problem that back-propagation allows the gradient to cause unnecessary deformations in the feature maps since the feature maps of the backbone network are used directly in bounding box regression and classification.
In the figure, we can see that SSD often detects a single object with two overlapping boxes.
However, these structures have the disadvantage of increasing the computational complexity, thus reduces detection speed, which is a key advantage of a single-stage detector.

background.summary: The work sits in the SSD multi-scale one-stage lineage (YOLO as the single-layer predecessor, SSD's lower-level features, R-SSD's rainbow concatenation and StairNet's unified prediction) and contrasts against two-stage R-CNN methods and the DSSD/FPN/RetinaNet accuracy fixes that trade speed away.

relatedWork.name: SSD
relatedWork.relation: base one-stage detector that RUN extends with residual blocks and unified prediction
relatedWork.quote: In order to solve this problem, SSD [17] utilized not only the highest-level features but also lower-level features which have enough resolution to detect small objects.

relatedWork.name: YOLO
relatedWork.relation: earlier single-stage method limited to highest-level features
relatedWork.quote: However, since YOLO uses only the highest-level1 feature maps to detect objects, there is a lack of lower-level information, which results in somewhat inaccurate detection, especially for small objects.

relatedWork.name: DSSD
relatedWork.relation: ResNet-101 + deconvolution accuracy fix that degrades speed
relatedWork.quote: DSSD [6] could obtain higher accuracy by changing the base network to ResNet-101 [10] and combining the FPN [14] using deconvolution layers in combination with the existing multiple layers to reflect the large scale context.

relatedWork.name: Recurrent Rolling Convolution (RRC)
relatedWork.relation: prior multi-scale context method that concatenates adjacent maps via pooling/deconvolution with an RNN
relatedWork.quote: RRC made multi-scale feature maps include large and small context by concatenating adjacent feature maps by pooling and deconvolution.

relatedWork.name: Rainbow SSD (R-SSD)
relatedWork.relation: closest prior art: cross-layer concatenation enabling a single unified prediction module
relatedWork.quote: Rainbow SSD (R-SSD) [11] proposed a method to concatenate feature maps not only in the adjacent layers but also in all the layers for bounding box regression and classification using pooling and deconvolution.

relatedWork.name: StairNet
relatedWork.relation: combines FPN on VGG-16 with R-SSD-style unified prediction
relatedWork.quote: Woo et al. [27] proposed StairNet which utilizes both FPN [14] structure of base VGG-16 network and unified prediction of R-SSD.

relatedWork.name: RetinaNet / Focal Loss
relatedWork.relation: state-of-the-art accuracy route via loss redesign with ResNet and FPN
relatedWork.quote: Their RetinaNet which uses Focal Loss in combination with ResNet and FPN [14] structure achieved the state-of-the-art performance.

evidence.quote: Thus, although classification may be relatively accurate, these are too slow to be used for real-time applications.
Recently, real-time detectors with low computational complexities have been actively researched.

solution.summary: RUN (Residual features and Unified prediction Network) inserts multi-way residual blocks (2-way, or 3-way with a deconvolution branch) between the reduced VGG-16 backbone and the heads as a gradient 'bumper' that decouples backbone features from detection, enriches each scale with cross-scale context, and then applies one unified prediction module across all now-equal-depth (256-dim) feature maps.
solution.approach: Decouple backbone from prediction with shared-depth multi-way Resblocks (including a deconvolution branch for large context), then predict with a single unified classifier over all scales.
components: 3-way Resblock: branch1 (1x1 conv + 3x3 conv), branch2 (3x3 conv for peripheral context), branch3 (deconvolution from the consecutive larger-scale layer)
all Resblock branches normalize feature depth to 256 so scales share information level
unified prediction module: one classifier shared over all multi-scale feature maps, 6 default boxes per layer
Resblock acts as a bumper, blocking prediction-module gradients from flowing into the backbone
staged training: fine-tune the 3-way model from a trained 2-way model with the prediction module unfrozen
reduced VGG-16 backbone pre-trained on ILSVRC CLS-LOC

evidence.quote: we propose a method to enrich the representation power of feature maps using Resblock and deconvolution layers.
In addition, a unified prediction module is applied to generalize output results and boost earlier layers' representation power for prediction.
Instead of directly connecting the feature maps in the backbone network to the prediction module, we inserted a multi-way Resblock for each level of feature maps, which acts like a bumper.
This prevents the gradients of the prediction module from flowing directly into the feature maps of the backbone network.

Because unified prediction applies equally to feature maps of all scales, it forces the output of the 3-way Resblock between the feature map of the backbone and the prediction module to be learned at a similar information level.

experiments.summary: Built on the public SSD codebase with reduced VGG-16, evaluated on PASCAL VOC 2007/2012 and MS COCO: an ablation over 2-way/3-way Resblock and unified prediction on VOC2007, VOC2012 comparisons against SSD/DSSD/R-SSD/StairNet, COCO test-dev comparisons including RetinaNet and two-stage methods, and a speed/accuracy study with FPS measured on Titan X and Titan X Pascal.

evidence.quote: we observed that the proposed model with only 2-way Resblock without the deconvolution path achieved 1.1% higher mAP than that of SSD.
RUN3WAY300 achieved 2.9% better mAP compared to SSD300 [17].
Also, RUN3WAY512 achieved 3.6% better mAP than SSD512.
RUN3WAY512 achieved the highest average precision and recall for small objects among compared methods except RetinaNet.

limitations.summary: End-to-end training of the 3-way model is worse than staged fine-tuning; with a shallow VGG-16 backbone RUN trails DSSD513 on COCO; accuracy gains cost speed relative to plain SSD; and the model sometimes merges a group of objects into one large box.
items: End-to-end training of the 3-way model produced worse results than the staged 2-way-then-3-way fine-tuning strategy.
RUN3WAY512 performs slightly worse than DSSD513, attributed to the shallower VGG-16 backbone versus ResNet-101.
RUN3way-300 is 36% slower than SSD300 in exchange for +2.9 mAP.
The method often detects a single large box covering a group of objects.
Some FPS numbers in the speed table are self-measured rather than taken from original papers.

evidence.quote: The end-to-end training was also applied on the 3-way model, but the results were worse than the above training strategy.
It performs slightly worse than DSSD513 [6], which is probably because the ResNet101 [10] backbone of DSSD513 produces better features for larger input images than VGG-16 [25] of SSD and ours.
The RUN-3way-300 model (25.0ms, 28.0% mAP) is 36% slower but 2.9% better in mAP than the SSD300 [17] model (18.3ms, 25.1% mAP).
Our method often detects a large box which covers a group of objects.

futureDirections.direction: Apply the Resblock + unified prediction design beyond SSD to other architectures that use multi-scale features.
futureDirections.quote: We expect the proposed method be not restricted to SSD-based methods but also applicable to other structures utilizing multi-scale features.

deploymentClaims: The full RUN3WAY512 model runs in real time (29.8 FPS) on Titan X Pascal, keeping the speed advantage of single-stage detection while adding residual context.
Measured on the same environment, RUN outperforms competitors with less loss of speed (e.g. about 60% faster than ResNet-101 SSD321 at similar mAP).

evidence.quote: Table 5 shows that even the most complex version of our method, RUN3WAY512, can works in real time (29.8 FPS) on Tital X Pascal.
Table5 shows that our method outperforms other competitors with less loss of speed.
